query: Starting from a multi-element automotive alloy catalyst containing multiple principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios, what single intervention could overcome activity loss and durability limitations while maintaining low platinum-group-metal consumption during transient and low-temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust operation, including exposure to H2O and NO and degradation associated with thermal aging or increasing mileage? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the untreated starting catalyst, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of nitrogen doping in a high-entropy alloy (HEA) catalyst, specifically in a Pt-rich skin supported on Vulcan XC-72 carbon, can overcome activity loss and durability limitations while maintaining low platinum-group-metal consumption during transient and low-temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust operation.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element automotive alloy catalyst containing multiple principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios
generation.intervention: Nitrogen doping in the HEA catalyst
generation.conditions: Transient and low-temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust operation, including exposure to H2O and NO and degradation associated with thermal aging or increasing mileage
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of multiple M-N bonds, which synergistically promote ORR performance
generation.mechanism: The introduction of nitrogen doping in the HEA catalyst leads to the formation of multiple M-N bonds, which enhances the durability of the catalyst and contributes to the improvement of catalytic activity by regulating the interaction between surface Pt and reactants
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced ORR performance, improved durability, and maintained low platinum-group-metal consumption
generation.boundary: Temperature range of 20-650°C, presence of H2O and NO, and increasing mileage
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of how nitrogen doping affects the HEA catalyst's performance is not fully understood and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the ORR performance and durability of N-doped HEA catalysts with untreated HEA catalysts under identical conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the N-doped HEA catalysts do not exhibit significantly improved ORR performance and durability compared to the untreated HEA catalysts, the hypothesis is falsified

Significantly, compared to binary or ternary alloys (e.g., solid-solution and intermetallic Pt alloys), HEA provides a broad binding energy distribution due to the large flexibility composition enabling a wide range of adsorption sites for multistep reaction (e.g., ORR), thereby achieving extraordinary catalytic performance.− The high entropy alloy also lowers the Gibbs free energy, which results in a more positive redox potential and consequently leads to enhanced stability of HEA catalysts. Additionally, nitrogen (N)-doping effects fine-tune the adsorption energetics of intermediates and improve the corrosion resistance by exploiting the pinning effect from the N atom to the coordinated metal atoms. ## Structure and Morphology Characterization
The structure evolution and formation of the HEA/C catalyst during the heat treatment were first investigated by in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD) using a wavelength of 0.6199 Å. A powder of metal precursors (Pt, Co, Fe, Ni, and Cu) mixed with the Vulcan XC-72 carbon black was annealed under a flow of 10 vol % H2/He. Based on the results of in situ XRD, the process of structure evolution of the HEA/C can be divided into three stages (Figure 1a). The disappearance of the original diffraction peaks indicates the metal precursors (mainly Pt) are reduced at stage I (20∼250 °C), which is followed by the emergence of a face-centered cubic (fcc) Pt phase at around 250 °C (marked by a black circle). As the energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mappings of N-HEA/C show (Figure S1), TM oxides formed on the surface, most likely induced by exposure to air after annealing. Thus, a post-acid treatment was necessary to remove the surface metal oxides (Figure S2) and then the N-doped HEA/C catalysts with Pt-rich shells (N–Pt/HEA/C) were obtained. For comparison, the HEA/C sample without N-doping (Pt-HEA/C) was also prepared by using the same acid treatment. Both the atomic ratios (Pt:Co:Ni:Fe:Cu) of HEA/C and N-HEA/C are close to 1:1:1:1:1, as determined by the scanning transmission electron microscopy EDS (STEM-EDS) analysis (Table S1), and the concentration of N dopants for N-HEA/C and N–Pt/HEA/C are 3.6 and 3.1 at. %, respectively. After acid-washing, the atomic ratios of the TMs in N–Pt/HEA/C are higher than those in Pt/HEA/C (Table S1), suggesting that the corrosion resistance of N–Pt/HEA/C was improved, possibly due to the formation of M-N bonds. The Pt L3-edge of N–Pt/HEA/C is slightly shifted to higher energy when compared to a reference Pt foil, and the WL intensity reduced (Figure 2a), indicating that the electronic and structure properties of Pt have been modified by alloying with the TMs. The extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra at the Pt L3-edge also showed that the bonding environment of Pt in the N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst is quite different from that in Pt foil (Figure S6), implying the presence of other metallic elements in the surrounding structure, which agrees with the nature of the Pt-based alloy. Similar results were found in the Pt L3-edge of Pt/HEA/C. After N-doping, the WL intensity of the Pt L3-edge for N–Pt/HEA/C is slightly higher than that of Pt/HEA/C, further proving that N dopants can fine-tune the atomic structure of Pt and therefore optimize the catalytic performance of N–Pt/HEA/C.

Compared with the Pt/HEA/C sample, the WL intensity of the XANES spectra at Co, Ni, Fe, and Cu K-edge for N–Pt/HEA/C were found to increase after N-doping (Figures 2b,e). This change is probably due to the partial electron migration from Co, Ni, Fe, and Cu atoms to N atoms because of the high electronegative difference between the 3d TMs and N element, leading to the formation of strong chemical bonds (multiple M-N bonds). This notion is also supported by the XANES results of relevant binary alloys. Although the actual structure of a solid-solution alloy comprising multielements with different radii could be rather distorted with local lattice strains, as shown schematically in Figure 2j, here, we consider a simple atomic model with equal lattice distances (Figure 2h). With an increase in doped N atoms, the core structure is distorted locally through the introduction of either expanded or contracted lattices; however, the lattice expansion of the fully coordinated atoms inside the core/bulk is restricted, resulting in the slight contraction of average lattice bonds. On the other hand, the structure of low-coordinated atoms at the surface can be influenced by lattice changes in the subsurface. When N atoms are introduced in subsurface layers of the core, the N atoms can cause expansion of the surface Pt atoms (Figure 2i). As discussed later, the formation of numerous M–N bonds and concomitant lattice disorder could enhance the durability of the catalyst, while the lattice expansion in surface Pt atoms could contribute to the improvement of catalytic activity.
